cases.title: Postgres index tips
cases.description:
3 Postgres performance fixes I use on every project:
- CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY so writes are not blocked
- EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) before and after every change
- Replace OFFSET pagination with keyset pagination: WHERE id > $last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 50
segments: okay three post grass performance fixes number one when you create an index use create index concurrently otherwise you lock the table for rights
number two always run explain analyze with buffers before and after so you see the actual numbers not guesses
number three stop using offset for pagination it gets slower the deeper you go use key set pagination where I D is greater than the last I D order by I D limit fifty

segments: welcome back to the show today we are talking about shipping faster with coding agents. Dana thinks the biggest win is not speed but fewer context switches. one thing that really changed my debugging, there is a Claude Code skill called systematic-debugging, it forces the agent to reproduce the bug and write down a hypothesis before touching any code. I only found it last week. Anyway. Marcus what about meetings.

Marcus says he blocks mornings for deep work and does no meetings before noon. Dana says burnout is the real risk with agents because the pace never drops. They agree to cap work in progress at three tasks. Marcus recommends the book Four Thousand Weeks by Oliver Burkeman for thinking about limits. They also discuss how on call rotations should change when agents ship code at night.

cases.title: Why we should stop measuring developer productivity by commits
segments: char=0-900

Counting commits to measure developer productivity is a mistake, and the reason is Goodhart's law: once a measure becomes a target it stops being a good measure. At one company the author describes, commit counts per developer rose 40% within a quarter after they were added to a dashboard, while shipped features per quarter fell from 11 to 8. Developers split work into tiny commits and avoided hard refactors that produce a single large change.

The author makes three arguments. First, commits measure activity, not value: a one line fix to a payment bug can matter more than a month of churn. Second, the metric punishes collaboration, because pairing and review produce no commits for the reviewer. Third, it hides the real constraint, which in the cases described was waiting time between review and deploy, a median of 3 days.

Critics reply that some quantitative signal is needed for management. The author concedes this and suggests DORA metrics instead: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. The author notes these should be tracked per team, never per individual, and still carry the risk of gaming.

cases.title: Harbour Ferries suspends service after hull inspection
segments: char=0-700

Harbour Ferries said on Tuesday 14 October it was suspending all sailings on the Kestrel route after an inspection found cracks in the hull of the MV Linnet. The company confirmed 212 passengers were on board when the cracks were reported on 9 October and that nobody was hurt. The Linnet, built in 1998, carries up to 340 passengers.

Transport minister Priya Anand said the suspension would last at least 3 weeks and that the ferry operator would receive no compensation for lost fares. A union representative, Tom Reyes, alleged that two earlier inspection reports in 2023 had flagged corrosion and were not acted on. Harbour Ferries denied this and said the 2023 reports found only cosmetic wear. The claim has not been verified. Replacement buses will run every 20 minutes from Wednesday and cost 4.50 pounds per trip, the same as the ferry fare.

cases.title: Choosing a message queue
segments: char=0-600

# Choosing a message queue

For most teams the decision comes down to ordering guarantees and operational cost. Our recommendation: start with a managed queue unless you need replay.

| Queue | Ordering | Replay | Max message size | Ops cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Amazon SQS Standard | best effort | no | 256 KB | none |
| Amazon SQS FIFO | strict per group | no | 256 KB | none |
| Apache Kafka | strict per partition | yes | 1 MB default | high |
| RabbitMQ | per queue | no | 128 MB | medium |

Pick Kafka only if consumers must re-read history or you need more than 100,000 messages per second. Pick SQS FIFO when order matters per customer. Avoid RabbitMQ lazy queues for payloads near the 128 MB limit because memory pressure causes stalls.

cases.title: Sparse attention for long documents
segments: page=1

Abstract. We propose WindowSparse, a sparse attention pattern combining local windows of 512 tokens with 8 global tokens per layer. On the LongDocQA benchmark WindowSparse reaches 71.4 F1, compared with 68.9 for full attention, while using 3.1x less memory at 16k tokens.
page=4

Table 2. Memory at 16k tokens: full attention 38.2 GB, WindowSparse 12.3 GB. Training used 64 A100 GPUs for 9 days. We note that the improvement over full attention is within one standard deviation on three of the five tasks.
page=7
Limitations. WindowSparse underperforms on tasks requiring long-range exact copy, dropping to 41.0 F1 on the SyntheticCopy task versus 88.5 for full attention. We did not evaluate beyond 32k tokens.

cases.title: Talk: scaling our search cluster
segments: when we started our search cluster had 6 nodes and we thought sharding by customer was the answer, it handled 2,000 queries per second.
sharding by customer turned out to be a mistake: one huge customer made one shard hot and p99 latency hit 900 ms. so we switched to sharding by document id hash.

quick correction to what I said earlier, the original cluster had 8 nodes not 6. after the switch p99 dropped to 120 ms and we moved to 12 nodes. the lesson is do not shard on a key whose distribution you do not control.
